newsitem.title: FRANCE: France hopes for quick sale of Thomson-CSF.
newsitem.headline: France hopes for quick sale of Thomson-CSF.

text.p: France, which has relaunched the privatisation of state electronics group Thomson SA, said South Korea's Daewoo could still be a candidate despite being ruled out in the first botched attempt to sell off the company.
"I want to dispell all misunderstanding...The government is taking every step to convince the Koreans that there was no prejudice involved," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said.

Just a week after scrapping its original privatisation plan, the government said on Wednesday it would privatise Thomson, but this time in two halves -- selling its profitable defence arm Thomson-CSF first and then money-losing consumer electronics division Thomson Multimedia.
Arthuis told reporters there was "no reason why Daewoo should be excluded" from the list of suitors for Thomson Multimedia but it "would depend on the formula" used for the privatisation."

The government scuttled the Thomson group's sale to Lagardere following objections by the French privatisation commission to the missile-to-publishing group's plans to spin off Thomson Multimedia to Daewoo because of worries over the transfer of technology.
South Korean industry leaders have slammed the decision as unfair and discriminatory and hinted there could be repercussions for French business in the booming Asian economy.
The government said it now plans to sell Thomson CSF "in the early months of 1997". Its 58-percent stake in Thomson CSF has a stock market value of around 11 billion francs.

Debt-laden Thomson Multimedia would be sold off later after implementation of a recovery plan and a 9.9 billion franc recapitalisation, Arthuis told reporters. "We need to do it as soon as possible but do it as well as possible," he said.
Daewoo, which would have become the biggest television set maker in the world with the acquisition of Thomson Multimedia, has been quoted as saying it is still interested in the company.

Arthuis said there was no decision on whether the privatisations would be through a company-to-company sale as planned previously or a public share offering. But an announcement on how the sale of Thomson CSF will be implemented is expected in the next few days.
The key thing was to "adapt the procedure to interest the staff in the privatisations," Arthuis said. Thomson workers have vociferously protested the group's sell-off.

The need to involve employees might be met, he suggested, by privatisation similar to that of computer-maker Bull last year. In that sale, part of the capital was set aside for staff and the rest earmarked for private placements.

Industrial conglomerate Alcatel Alsthom, whose offer for Thomson was rejected by the government in favour of Lagardere's, said on Thursday it was still interested in Thomson CSF but wanted to see the terms.
Lagardere has made no comment about its plans but Prime Minister Alain Juppe stressed this week "the industrial logic" of the Lagardere missile group taking over Thomson CSF.
Arthuis said he was aware of possible threats to French investment in South Korea from the escalating row and said he hoped the recent events would not send out wrong message.
"France cannot develop without being open to the rest of the world," he said. "It cannot retreat into itself."
Privately a senior government offical said the government had been "astonished" by the decision of the privatisation commission to oppose the sale.
